question_text:
A 15-year-old girl is hospitalized because of increased fatigue and weight loss over the past 2 months. The patient has no personal or family history of a serious illness. She takes no medications, currently. Her blood pressure is 175/74 mm Hg on the left arm and 90/45 on the right. The radial pulse is 84/min but weaker on the right side. The femoral blood pressure and pulses show no abnormalities. Temperature is 38.1℃ (100.6℉). The muscles over the right upper arm are slightly atrophic. The remainder of the examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show the following results:
Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL
Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h
Magnetic resonance arteriography reveals irregularity, stenosis, and poststenotic dilation involving the proximal right subclavian artery. Prednisone is initiated with improvement of her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the patient management?

                    ### Question
                    A 15-year-old girl is hospitalized because of increased fatigue and weight loss over the past 2 months. The patient has no personal or family history of a serious illness. She takes no medications, currently. Her blood pressure is 175/74 mm Hg on the left arm and 90/45 on the right. The radial pulse is 84/min but weaker on the right side. The femoral blood pressure and pulses show no abnormalities. Temperature is 38.1℃ (100.6℉). The muscles over the right upper arm are slightly atrophic. The remainder of the examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show the following results:
Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL
Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h
Magnetic resonance arteriography reveals irregularity, stenosis, and poststenotic dilation involving the proximal right subclavian artery. Prednisone is initiated with improvement of her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the patient management?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Carvedilol + hydrochlorothiazide
opb. Cyclophosphamide
opc. Plasmapheresis
opd. Rituximab
ope. Surgery

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 15-year-old girl presents with symptoms suggestive of a vascular issue, specifically vasculitis, indicated by the irregularity and stenosis of the right subclavian artery seen on MRI. The elevated blood pressure on the left arm and lower blood pressure on the right arm, along with a weaker pulse on the right side, further support this diagnosis. Prednisone was initiated and led to symptom improvement, which is consistent with the treatment of vasculitis. The next step in management should consider the severity of the condition and the response to initial therapy. Cyclophosphamide is indicated for severe cases of vasculitis, especially if there is significant vascular involvement or if the patient does not respond adequately to corticosteroids alone. While rituximab is an option for refractory cases, it is typically considered after cyclophosphamide in severe cases. Surgical intervention is generally reserved for specific complications or persistent symptoms despite medical management. Plasmapheresis is less common for this condition and is not typically the first-line treatment. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to consider cyclophosphamide for further treatment of the vasculitis.
